title: Find the seam
context: A history student is writing about how Britain came to use a single standard time.
question: Click the word where Whitcombe's idea ends and the writer's own point begins.
text: By the late 1840s, most British railway companies had adopted London time, and many towns along their lines gradually followed. {{cite:whitcombe2016|integral}} {{v:argues|argued}} that this shift was driven less by public demand than by the practical problem of printing timetables that passengers could trust. {{seam}}This would explain why many towns on a railway line changed their public clocks before the law required them to. If Whitcombe is right, standard time was not a national decision imposed from above but a commercial habit that spread along the tracks. That interpretation also helps to explain why legal recognition came so late, in 1880, long after most clocks had already changed.

feedback.correct: Yes. Whitcombe's argument is the sentence that names her. From 'This would explain…' onwards, the writer is applying her idea and drawing their own conclusions from it.
feedback.early: A reasonable instinct, but you've split Whitcombe's own claim. Everything in the sentence that names her is her argument, reported by the writer.
feedback.late: You've given Whitcombe more than she said. 'This would explain…' is the writer using her idea to explain something — that's the writer's voice, even though it depends on her argument.

followUp.question: What signals the seam most clearly in this paragraph?

options.text: The word 'This', which points back to Whitcombe's claim and starts doing something with it.
options.feedback: Yes. 'This would explain…' and 'If Whitcombe is right…' are the writer's moves: applying the source, then testing it.

Partly. Here the author is named at the start of the sentence, so the citation tells you where the source begins but not where it ends. In footnote styles the note marker falls at the end of the sentence, which helps. Either way, the clearest signal is the writer's own wording.
Tense can help, but here it doesn't really mark the seam. Look at what the sentence after the citation is doing with Whitcombe's idea.

notes.text: In footnote styles, the note marker comes at the end of the sentence that reports the source — here, just before the seam. Readers rely on your wording, not the footnote, to see where your own point begins.

chefsNote: Every good sauce has a seam: the point where the cook takes over.
